answer.sourceLine: The line comes verbatim from Chapter 6 of Austen's Northanger Abbey (1817), confirmed against the Project Gutenberg and Wikisource texts — though it is spoken by the character Isabella Thorpe, not offered as Austen's own statement of belief.

docMeta.dd: Isabella Thorpe, in conversation with Catherine Morland

source.excerpt: “Yes, that I do. There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends. I have no notion of loving people by halves; it is not my nature. My attachments are always excessively strong.”
trail: First published posthumously by John Murray on 20 December 1817, six months after Austen's death, alongside Persuasion — confirmed by Austen historian Susannah Fullerton ↗.
The sentence appears verbatim in both the Project Gutenberg text ↗, which prints a semicolon after “halves,” and the Wikisource edition ↗, whose transcription prints a comma there.
The speaker is Isabella Thorpe, a character Wikipedia's summary ↗ describes as insincere and self-interested, whose loyalty evaporates once her own prospects are at stake.
Austen scholar Deborah Yaffe has written about how this line is routinely stripped of its ironic context ↗ and repackaged as sincere Austen wisdom.
source.excerptNote: Isabella says this moments after boasting that she publicly scolded a man for not sufficiently admiring her friend — the kind of loud, performative devotion Austen spends the rest of the novel quietly dismantling.
source.rightsNote: Northanger Abbey was first published in 1817 and has long been in the public domain in the United States; the text above is drawn from the public-domain Project Gutenberg edition.

context.heading: Why a hypocrite's line became a friendship quote
lead: Northanger Abbey was Jane Austen's earliest completed novel, written around 1798–99, but it went unpublished until December 1817, six months after her death. Alongside its send-up of Gothic fiction, the book is full of Austen's characteristic skewering of social performance — nowhere more so than in Isabella Thorpe.

Isabella delivers this declaration of boundless loyalty in the pump-room, moments after recounting how she publicly scolded a man at a dance for not sufficiently admiring her friend. It reads as a performance of devotion rather than evidence of it: later in the novel Isabella drops her engagement to Catherine's brother the moment a wealthier prospect appears — the opposite of the unwavering “attachments” she claims here.
context.detailsSummary: Why Isabella Thorpe's words don't match her actions
detailsBody: Isabella becomes engaged to James Morland, Catherine's brother, but soon begins flirting with the wealthier Captain Frederick Tilney; when the engagement stalls over money, she drops James to pursue Tilney instead — the opposite of the “my attachments are always excessively strong” she claims in this same speech.
context.pull: The words are Austen's. The sincerity is Isabella Thorpe's performance.
